positions.commentary: Veeva Systems is acknowledged as a large public company in healthcare but is explicitly stated to be not worth as much as Epic.
Microsoft is mentioned as a partner of Epic and a buyer of Nuance, having an ambient AI product for healthcare.
Amazon is mentioned as a company that needs to be careful about going too far into one customer segment when building horizontal software.

thesis: The episode argues that Epic Systems is the dominant and most valuable vertical market software company globally, possessing a wide moat through its integrated platform, regulatory advantages, and status as the industry's essential choke point. The speakers contend that Epic's incumbency will be further strengthened by new interoperability standards and its ability to extract increasing value from its install base, while explicitly noting that competitors like Veeva are not worth as much.

claims.claim: The speakers argue that Epic is a dominant vertical market software company with a strong moat due to its integrated platform, regulatory compliance advantages, and deep customer relationships.
claims.quote: I think it's the same question here. To me it just smacked me in the head. This is vertical market software. This is the correct playbook to win in vertical market software, and it is very different from building horizontal market software.

claims.claim: Epic is described as the choke point of the healthcare industry, controlling access to hospital systems for new software innovations.
claims.quote: Epic is the choke point of the industry at this point to decide what software innovations reach hospitals. I don't think it's overstating it to say if you're developing new breakthrough software to be used by physicians in hospital systems, Epic's the one that gets to decide, are you going to reach that customer or not.

claims.claim: Regulation and interoperability standards like TEFCA are expected to further entrench Epic as an incumbent with resources to comply.
claims.quote: Honestly, at this point, regulation is probably also a bull case. This is what happens once you become an incumbent. Regulation tends to shut out new entrants and entrench the older companies because the older companies are the ones that have the resources to comply.

claims.claim: Epic has significant pricing power and can extract more value from its install base as it becomes the standard.
claims.quote: They've become the standard that everyone will switch to once they get a customer. They don't leave. Honestly, at this point, regulation is probably also a bull case.

claims.claim: Epic is considered the most valuable vertical market software company in the world, surpassing competitors like Veeva Systems.
claims.quote: Then I was thinking about it and I was like, Epic has got to be the most valuable vertical market software company in the entire world. What else could possibly be up there?

claims.claim: Veeva Systems is acknowledged as a large public company in healthcare but is explicitly stated to be not worth as much as Epic.
claims.quote: But then I was Googling and I was thinking about it. I was like, well people talk about Veeva Systems. Ben: Yeah, Veeva, which is also healthcare. David: They're probably the largest public company. But I was like yep, they're definitely not worth as much as Epic, and they're also operating in healthcare.

claims.claim: Microsoft is mentioned as a partner of Epic and a buyer of Nuance, having an ambient AI product for healthcare.
claims.quote: David: That's right. One is Microsoft and Nuance. Microsoft bought a company called Nuance a few years ago. Ben: They used to do Dragon Dictation? David: Yeah. They've always been in the voice space for healthcare. They now have an ambient AI product.

claims.claim: Amazon is mentioned as a company that needs to be careful about going too far into one customer segment when building horizontal software.
claims.quote: David: Because in vertical market software, you are only serving one category of user. The deeper and deeper and deeper you can go into their business operations and solving their problems, the better. Whereas if you're building Slack or Salesforce…
